One average return, many ending balances: read the distribution behind a projection

Use a percentile fan, outcome-probability bars, a mean-versus-median comparison and a sensitivity matrix to understand an assumed range of investment outcomes.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore an assumed return distribution

Interactive planning lab

Median ending balance in the assumed model$105,935.06
Mean ending balance in the assumed model$132,664.89
Model probability of ending below the selected balance46.58%

Original mathematical illustration for one positive starting amount, with no later cash flows. Annual gross return is lognormally distributed; log gross returns are independent, normally distributed and identically parameterised across years. The entered mean is the expected simple annual return. Log-return mean equals ln(1 + mean simple return) minus half the squared log-return standard deviation. The volatility input is the standard deviation of log gross return, not the standard deviation of the simple percentage return. Parameters are assumed and are not fitted to any market, fund or security. Every probability is conditional on this chosen distribution; none estimates your real-world likelihood of meeting a goal. Dollar amounts and the goal are nominal, before fees, taxes and inflation. Quantiles are calculated analytically, without random simulation or a historical sample. A normal-CDF numerical approximation is used for probabilities. The zero-volatility case collapses to one deterministic balance; below means strictly below, while equality meets the comparison amount.

The central idea

An average return can produce an attractive average ending balance while leaving a substantial lower tail. The distribution and its assumptions matter as much as the central number.

01

A smooth projection answers a narrower question than a household goal

A calculator can turn CAD 50,000 into CAD 132,664.89 after twenty years at a constant 5% annual return. That arithmetic is correct. It does not establish that an investor will receive a smooth 5% each year or have that particular amount when a bill is due.

The charts add an explicit distribution around a single starting amount. They assume a 5% mean simple annual return and a 15% standard deviation of annual log returns. Under those assumptions, the model’s mean ending balance is still CAD 132,664.89, but its median is about CAD 105,935.06. The difference comes from the distribution’s shape, rather than different deposits or a hidden fee.

This is an original mathematical example. No historical market series is used, the parameters are not estimated for any investment, and the tool does not select securities. The purpose is to show what a probability statement depends on before treating it as evidence that a real goal is adequately funded.

02

Read one vertical slice of the fan at a time

The first chart shades two ranges. The outer band connects the 5th and 95th percentiles at each year. The inner band connects the 25th and 75th percentiles. The dark line follows the median. All begin at the same starting capital because no investment uncertainty has accumulated at time zero.

At the default twenty-year finish, the 5th percentile is about CAD 35,142.98 and the 95th percentile about CAD 319,330.83. Under the assumed continuous distribution, 5% of final balances lie below the first value and 5% above the second. Neither endpoint is a guaranteed minimum or maximum. A positive mean return does not rule out ending with less than the initial amount.

The lines are pointwise summaries, not examples of actual market paths. The investor occupying the median rank in year five need not occupy that rank in year twenty. A central 90% range at each date also does not establish that 90% of entire investment paths remain inside the shaded band for every year.

03

The mean and median are different summaries, not competing forecasts

The median splits a continuous probability distribution into two equal parts. The mean is the probability-weighted average of all its values. A right-skewed distribution can contain relatively infrequent large balances that pull the mean above the median.

With the default inputs, the mean is about 25.23% above the median. That does not mean the model has discovered a free investment premium. The upper tail is part of the same assumed distribution that also contains disappointing outcomes. Removing that tail from the explanation while retaining its effect on the mean would give a misleading picture.

The summary bars place the 5th percentile, median, mean and 95th percentile beside each other. The mean is not another percentile and need not sit halfway between the endpoints. When the volatility assumption is set to zero, uncertainty disappears from this model: all four values collapse to the same deterministic balance. That is a mathematical control, not evidence that any actual product can deliver the selected return without risk.

04

A model probability is conditional on the model you chose

The default nominal comparison amount is CAD 100,000. The model places about 46.58% of ending balances below it. This result is conditional on every stated input and distributional assumption; it is not a measured failure frequency for Canadian investors or an assessment of anyone’s personal chance of success.

The outcome-range bars divide all possible non-negative ending balances into disjoint intervals. Each range includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper boundary. The final range includes everything at or above its lower boundary. Their unrounded probabilities add to 100%, and the ranges do not discard the far upper tail.

Read these as categorical probability bars. The dollar intervals have different widths, so their bar areas should not be interpreted as a continuous histogram density. Changing the goal changes the interval boundaries and the comparison probability; it does not change the underlying wealth distribution. The data tables preserve the range labels and values so that the visible statement can be checked.

05

Know which return the formula treats as the mean

Let r be the assumed mean simple annual return and s the standard deviation of annual log gross return, both expressed as fractions. The model sets the mean log gross return to m = ln(1 + r) − s² ÷ 2. It then assumes independent, identically distributed normal log gross returns in every year.

After T years, the log of the wealth multiple has mean Tm and standard deviation s√T. A percentile is starting capital × exp(Tm + s√T × z), where z is the corresponding standard-normal quantile. Expected ending wealth is starting capital × (1 + r)T. These relations explain why changing dispersion while preserving the expected simple return can change the median without changing the mean.

The NIST lognormal-distribution reference describes the underlying distribution, its quantiles and its distinct mean and median. TickerLantern applies those mathematical relationships to an original financial illustration. The volatility input is explicitly a log-return standard deviation; treating it as an interchangeable simple-return standard deviation would define a different model.

06

Use the sensitivity matrix to question the assumptions

The matrix changes log-return dispersion and the nominal balance being tested. Expected simple return, starting capital and horizon remain fixed. A different cell is a different conditional calculation, not stronger evidence that a target is safe. At zero dispersion, the result is either 0% or 100%, with equality counted as meeting the comparison amount.

Real returns need not be independent or normally distributed in log space. Market regimes, changing volatility, severe tail events, investment costs, taxes and inflation can materially change outcomes. Contributions and withdrawals would also change the wealth distribution and are deliberately absent here. A long horizon does not remove those modeling limitations.

FINRA’s discussion of investment-analysis tools illustrates why assumptions, methodology and the hypothetical nature of projected outcomes need clear explanation. It is cited as U.S. educational context, not as an endorsement of this tool or a determination of Canadian requirements. Before using an uncertain return to support an important payment, revisit the cash contribution, the date, the goal’s flexibility and what would happen if the balance were inadequate.
